claims.text: A critical transient mixing regime during heating governs formation of a single-phase solid solution in noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
An intermediate dwell or controlled ramp at a suitable temperature enhances interdiffusion while avoiding irreversible phase separation or thermal decomposition.
Enhanced interdiffusion during the proposed thermal stage enables homogeneous nucleation.
Homogeneous nucleation favors formation of a single-phase structure.
Under standard rapid heating and cooling, the precursor system tends to form multiphase nanoparticles or exhibit elemental segregation.
There is a temperature window in which diffusion is active while the thermodynamic driving force for segregation remains suppressed.
Significant atomic mobility begins below temperatures at which phase-separation or decomposition kinetics dominate.
The proposed intervention applies to noble-metal alloys containing more than five constituents under rapid heating and cooling.
Dwell time at the mixing temperature controls the extent of homogeneous interdiffusion relative to localized elemental segregation.
A controlled intermediate dwell provides enough atomic mobility for elemental intermixing.
Elemental intermixing produces uniform nucleation events that yield a metastable single-phase solid solution.
Rapid heating and cooling without the dwell provides insufficient time for interdiffusion.
Insufficient interdiffusion causes heterogeneous nucleation, elemental segregation, multiphase structure, or non-ideal particle morphology.
Nanoparticles produced with the intermediate dwell will have greater single-phase crystallinity than nanoparticles produced by the baseline rapid-heating protocol.
Nanoparticles produced with the intermediate dwell will exhibit less elemental segregation than the baseline.
The dwell-treated material will display a consistent crystallographic phase by X-ray diffraction.
The dwell-treated material will display a uniform distribution of all components by elemental mapping.
The hypothesis is limited to compositions having a narrow thermal-processing window.
The intervention may not be effective for compositions with drastically different elemental diffusivities.
